patient.name: Margaret Doyle
patient.setting: Acute medical ward (admitted after a fall)
patient.complaint: Found on the kitchen floor after a fall; eating very little for weeks
background: Widowed 6 months ago; lives alone in a flat in Tottenham
Lost about 9 kg over 4 months (usual weight 56 kg)
Daughter says the fridge was almost empty

diagnosis.exam: Expect a frail, isolated older person (or alcohol misuse, cancer or malabsorption) with weight loss and wasting, and named deficiencies: pellagra (4 Ds), night blindness (vitamin A). Refeeding syndrome is the classic complication.

points: Margaret, 82, lay on her kitchen floor overnight after a fall.
Clothes hang off her; rings slip off her fingers.
Daughter: she has 'barely eaten' since her husband died.
She has had **almost nothing to eat for over a week**.

steps.lead: Margaret's weight loss, wasting and falls are malnutrition: not enough **calories, protein and nutrients**, with loss of function.
Margaret ticks three boxes: **elderly, living alone, dementia**. Bereavement made her intake worse.

points: Temporal and shoulder **muscle wasting**; thin, sparse hair.
A grade 2 **pressure sore** over her sacrum from the long lie.
Height 1.60 m, weight 47 kg: BMI 18.4 kg/m².

steps.lead: Margaret shows the signs (wasting, hair thinning, pressure sore, oedema) and the symptoms (weight loss, falls, fatigue, lost independence).

visual.title: Margaret's BMI
visual.label: Margaret 18.4
visual.caption: BMI below 18.5 scores 2 on MUST by itself.

steps.q: Margaret has had almost no food for over a week. Which complication must the team plan for before feeding her?
steps.r: Days of minimal intake plus low BMI make her **high risk of refeeding syndrome**: feed slowly, give thiamine, watch phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

steps.lead: Margaret is exactly who gets **refeeding syndrome**: starved for days, then fed. Watch for **low phosphate, potassium, magnesium**.

steps.title: Deficiency patterns that come with malnutrition
head: Setting
Deficiency
Clue in the stem

steps.lead: Margaret's sacral sore needs **dietitian review, dressings and a pressure-relieving mattress**. The other conditions here are look-alikes and causes to spot in other stems.

steps.text: The **4 Ds of pellagra**: diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia, death. A dark band round the neck is **Casal's necklace**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate screening tool?' (MUST) and the albumin trap: a low albumin in a septic or cirrhotic patient does not measure nutrition.

steps.q: Margaret is admitted to the ward. How is her malnutrition risk screened?
steps.r: **MUST** is the validated UK screening tool. Waterlow scores pressure-sore risk; albumin is unreliable.

steps.lead: Margaret's **MUST**: BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute illness effect. Add a **dietary recall** from her daughter and **FBC, U&Es, LFTs**.

visual.title: Margaret's MUST score
visual.label: Margaret 6
visual.caption: BMI 18.4 (2) + 16% weight loss (2) + no intake likely for more than 5 days (2) = 6.

steps.title: Margaret's admission bloods
steps.text: Phosphate, potassium and magnesium are already low **before** feeding: her refeeding risk is very high.

steps.lead: Margaret's albumin of 28 is low, but her CRP is 64 (a chest infection), so **albumin cannot be trusted** as a nutrition marker.

steps.text: Do not pick 'serum albumin' as the test of nutritional status. It falls in **inflammation, sepsis and liver disease** too.

steps.lead: The dietitian's **clinical and nutritional assessment** of Margaret (history, examination, intake, function) confirms the diagnosis.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate next step?' with the feeding ladder (oral, then enteral NG/PEG, then parenteral) and refeeding prevention: start slowly with thiamine and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

steps.lead: Margaret's MUST is well above 2: **food-first plus oral nutritional supplements**, and **thiamine** because intake was absent for over 5 days.

steps.title: The feeding ladder
nodes: Oral: food first, fortified, high-calorie high-protein
Gut works but oral intake inadequate: NG tube
Gut cannot be used: parenteral nutrition (TPN)
steps.caption: Always use the gut if it works.

steps.lead: Margaret can swallow and her gut works, so she stays **oral**. The cause is treated too: bereavement, dementia support and help at home.

steps.q: Margaret is high risk of refeeding syndrome. How should feeding start?
o: Slowly, with thiamine and electrolyte replacement
steps.r: **Start low and go slow**, give **thiamine** before and during feeding, and monitor and replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium.

steps.lead: Margaret has low BMI, days of minimal intake and low electrolytes already: **start slowly, thiamine, replace phosphate, magnesium, potassium**.

visual.title: Margaret's phosphate in the first days of feeding
visual.caption: Phosphate falls once feeding starts (insulin surge); daily checks and IV replacement bring it back.

steps.text: Do not 'catch up' calories in a starved patient. Rapid feeding drives the **insulin surge** that causes arrhythmias, heart failure and seizures.

steps.lead: Margaret's screening and feeding follow **MUST (BAPEN)** and **NICE CG32** nutrition support in adults.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why phosphate falls in refeeding, why thiamine matters, why malabsorption causes A, D, E, K deficiency, and why niacin deficiency causes the 4 Ds.

steps.lead: Margaret has been **burning her own fat and muscle**. Low hepatic protein synthesis explains her low albumin and ankle oedema.
When Margaret eats again, **insulin** pushes phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and uses up her **thiamine**.

steps.title: Refeeding syndrome
nodes: Starvation: intracellular phosphate, K and Mg depleted
Glucose, phosphate, K, Mg driven into cells
Low serum levels: arrhythmia, heart failure, seizures
Thiamine used up: Wernicke's, wet beriberi

steps.q: Why must Margaret have thiamine before her feeds are increased?
o: It is a cofactor for carbohydrate metabolism
steps.r: **Thiamine (B1)** is a cofactor for carbohydrate metabolism and is used up fast on refeeding, risking **Wernicke's** and **wet beriberi**.

steps.lead: Not Margaret's problem, but in **coeliac disease** damaged mucosa and poor **micelle** uptake stop vitamins A, D, E and K being absorbed.
In **pellagra**, low niacin starves NAD/NADP-dependent energy pathways in fast-turnover tissues: skin, gut and brain.

steps.text: Map the 4 Ds to tissues: **dermatitis** (skin), **diarrhoea** (gut), **dementia** (CNS), then death.

mcq.q: Which electrolyte fall is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome?
mcq.r: **Low phosphate**, with low potassium and magnesium and thiamine deficiency.

mcq.q: Which are the 4 Ds of pellagra?
mcq.r: Pellagra (niacin, B3) gives **diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia, death**.

mcq.q: Night blindness in coeliac disease reflects deficiency of which vitamin?
mcq.r: **Vitamin A** is fat-soluble and malabsorbed in coeliac disease.

mcq.q: Which is the validated UK malnutrition screening tool?
mcq.r: **MUST** assesses BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect.

mcq.q: Why is albumin unreliable as a nutritional marker?
o: It falls in inflammation, sepsis and liver disease
It has a half-life of 2 hours
It is raised by dehydration only
It is not measured in UK labs
mcq.r: Albumin falls in **inflammation, sepsis and liver disease** regardless of nutrition.
**Clinical and nutritional assessment** is the gold standard.

mcq.q: A patient cannot eat enough but the gut works. What is the next step after oral supplements?
mcq.r: **Enteral** feeding (NG, PEG for longer term) if the gut is functional; TPN only if it is not.

mcq.q: Which vitamin is given before refeeding a high-risk patient?
mcq.r: **Thiamine** prevents Wernicke's encephalopathy and wet beriberi.

mcq.q: What drives phosphate into cells in refeeding syndrome?
mcq.r: Carbohydrate triggers an **insulin surge** that drives phosphate, K and Mg intracellularly.

mcq.q: Why does chronic protein-calorie deficiency cause oedema?
o: Sodium retention by the kidney alone
mcq.r: Less **albumin** is made, lowering oncotic pressure, so fluid leaks into tissues.

prompts.q: What is malnutrition, what causes it and who is at risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: spot the at-risk person in the first line of the stem.

points.p: Deficiency of calories, protein and essential nutrients
points.why: It causes weight loss, wasting and functional decline.

points.p: Causes: poor oral intake, chronic disease or cancer, malabsorption
points.why: Always look for the underlying cause.

points.p: Alcohol misuse and eating disorders
points.why: Both are high-risk for refeeding syndrome.

points.p: Elderly living alone, frailty, dementia, long-stay inpatients
points.why: The classic stem is a frail older person living alone.

prompts.q: List the signs and symptoms of malnutrition.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: falls, infections and poor healing are all clues.

points.p: Unintentional weight loss, low BMI, muscle wasting, cachexia
points.why: Over 10% unplanned loss scores 2 on MUST.

points.p: Hair thinning, pressure sores, poor wound healing
points.why: Pressure sores need nutrition, dressings and a supportive mattress.

points.p: Peripheral oedema in severe protein deficiency
Fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, falls, frequent infections, loss of independence
Electrolyte and micronutrient abnormalities, GI symptoms

prompts.q: What is pellagra, and which vitamin deficiencies come with coeliac disease and alcohol cirrhosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one clue (necklace rash, night blindness) names the vitamin.

points.p: Pellagra = niacin (B3) deficiency
4 Ds: diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia, death; Casal's necklace
points.why: Casal's necklace is a hyperpigmented band round the neck.

points.p: Coeliac: fat-soluble A, D, E, K deficiency; night blindness from vitamin A
Alcohol cirrhosis: B12, iron, albumin deficiencies (per notes)
points.why: The liver cannot absorb or process nutrients properly.

prompts.q: What is refeeding syndrome? Give the biochemical findings and the clinical features.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a patient who deteriorates after feeding starts.

points.p: Too-rapid feeding of a severely malnourished patient; insulin surge drives electrolytes into cells
points.why: Usually within the first few days of feeding.

points.p: Low phosphate
Low potassium and low magnesium
Thiamine deficiency
Weakness, confusion, seizures, arrhythmia, heart failure

prompts.q: How is malnutrition screened and confirmed? Name the tool, its three parts and the first bloods.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'screening' is MUST; 'gold standard' is clinical and nutritional assessment.

points.p: MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool)
BMI, % unplanned weight loss, acute disease effect (no intake likely for more than 5 days)
points.why: Each scores 0 to 2; a total of 2 or more is high risk.

points.p: Dietary recall and bloods: FBC, U&Es, LFTs
points.why: Look for electrolyte and micronutrient deficiencies.

points.p: Gold standard: clinical and nutritional assessment

prompts.q: Why is albumin not a reliable marker of nutrition?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a classic distractor in investigation questions.

points.p: Falls in inflammation and sepsis
points.why: It is a negative acute-phase protein.

points.p: Falls in liver disease

prompts.q: What is the first-line treatment for a high MUST score, and what is the stepwise feeding ladder?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: if the gut works, use it.

points.p: MUST 2 or more: food-first approach plus oral nutritional supplements
points.why: High-calorie, high-protein diet and fortified food.

points.p: Thiamine if intake poor or absent for more than 5 days
Treat the underlying cause
Enteral: NG tube, PEG for longer term, if gut functional
points.why: PEG for long-term needs such as head and neck cancer.

points.p: Parenteral nutrition (TPN) if the gut cannot be used

prompts.q: Who is at high risk of refeeding syndrome, and how do you prevent it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'before you start the NG feed' question.

points.p: High risk: low BMI, minimal intake for days, eating disorder, cancer or cachexia, alcohol misuse
points.why: Low electrolytes before feeding add to the risk.

points.p: Start feeding slowly
Give thiamine
Monitor and replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium
points.why: Daily bloods in the first days.

prompts.q: Explain the mechanism of refeeding syndrome and why thiamine matters.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: starvation, carbohydrate, insulin, shift.

points.p: Starvation depletes intracellular phosphate, K and Mg; body shifts to fat metabolism
points.why: Serum levels can look normal before feeding.

points.p: Carbohydrate triggers an insulin surge driving glucose, phosphate, K and Mg into cells
Thiamine is a cofactor for carbohydrate metabolism and is rapidly depleted
points.why: Deficiency causes Wernicke's encephalopathy or wet beriberi.

prompts.q: Why does malnutrition cause wasting and oedema, malabsorption cause A, D, E, K deficiency, and niacin deficiency cause the 4 Ds?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the sign in the stem.

points.p: Catabolism of fat and muscle causes wasting, immune dysfunction, poor healing
Reduced hepatic protein (albumin) synthesis causes oedema
Malabsorption reduces bile-salt and micelle uptake of fat-soluble vitamins
points.why: Damaged small bowel mucosa in coeliac disease.

points.p: Niacin deficiency impairs NAD/NADP energy metabolism in skin, gut, CNS

glossary.malnutrition: Deficiency of calories, protein and nutrients causing weight loss, wasting and loss of function.
glossary.MUST: Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool: scores BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect; 2 or more is high risk.
glossary.BAPEN: British Association for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition; developed MUST.
glossary.BMI: Body mass index: weight in kg divided by height in metres squared.
glossary.cachexia: Severe wasting of muscle and fat, often due to cancer or chronic disease.
glossary.muscle wasting: Visible loss of muscle bulk, e.g. at the temples, shoulders and hands.
glossary.pressure sore: Skin and tissue breakdown over a bony area from prolonged pressure.
glossary.Waterlow score: Tool that scores pressure-sore risk, not malnutrition.
glossary.dietary recall: Patient's report of everything eaten and drunk over a set period.
glossary.albumin: Main plasma protein made by the liver; low in malnutrition but also in inflammation and liver disease.
glossary.hypoalbuminaemia: Low blood albumin, lowering oncotic pressure and causing oedema.
glossary.oncotic pressure: Pull exerted by plasma proteins that keeps fluid in blood vessels.
glossary.oral nutritional supplements: Prescribed high-energy, high-protein drinks taken alongside food.
glossary.food-first: Improving intake with normal and fortified food before adding supplements.
glossary.food fortification: Adding extra energy and protein to normal food, e.g. cream, butter, milk powder.
glossary.enteral feeding: Feeding liquid nutrition directly into the gut through a tube.
glossary.NG tube: Nasogastric tube: passed through the nose into the stomach for short-term feeding.
glossary.PEG: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy: a tube through the abdominal wall into the stomach for long-term feeding.
glossary.parenteral nutrition: Intravenous feeding that bypasses the gut, used when the gut cannot be used.
glossary.TPN: Total parenteral nutrition: all nutritional needs given intravenously.
glossary.refeeding syndrome: Dangerous fall in phosphate, potassium and magnesium when a starved patient is fed too quickly.
glossary.hypophosphataemia: Low blood phosphate; the hallmark of refeeding syndrome.
glossary.hypokalaemia: Low blood potassium; can cause arrhythmias and weakness.
glossary.hypomagnesaemia: Low blood magnesium; causes arrhythmias, seizures and worsens low potassium.
glossary.thiamine: Vitamin B1: cofactor for carbohydrate metabolism, rapidly used up on refeeding.
glossary.Pabrinex: Intravenous high-dose B vitamin preparation including thiamine.
glossary.Wernicke's encephalopathy: Acute thiamine deficiency causing confusion, ataxia and eye movement problems.
glossary.wet beriberi: Thiamine deficiency causing high-output heart failure and oedema.
glossary.niacin: Vitamin B3; needed to make NAD and NADP for energy metabolism.
glossary.pellagra: Niacin deficiency causing diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia and death.
glossary.Casal's necklace: Hyperpigmented band of dermatitis around the neck in pellagra.
glossary.NAD: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide: niacin-derived coenzyme for cellular energy production.
glossary.coeliac disease: Immune reaction to gluten that damages the small bowel lining and causes malabsorption.
glossary.anti-endomysial antibodies: Antibodies used to test for coeliac disease.
glossary.malabsorption: Failure of the gut to absorb nutrients, e.g. coeliac disease or pancreatic insufficiency.
glossary.fat-soluble vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E and K, which need bile and micelles to be absorbed.
glossary.micelle: Bile-salt cluster that carries fats and fat-soluble vitamins to the gut wall.
glossary.night blindness: Poor vision in dim light from vitamin A deficiency.
glossary.catabolism: Breaking down body tissues (fat, muscle) for energy.
glossary.steatorrhoea: Pale, bulky, foul-smelling, greasy stool from fat malabsorption.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: blood marker that rises with inflammation and infection.

technique.stem: A 24 year old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted with a BMI of 13.5 kg/m². Nasogastric feeding is started at full calorie target. On day 3 she becomes weak and confused and has a seizure. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, irregular, and BP 96/60 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question in a patient who got worse after feeding started.
Severely malnourished, fed too fast, deteriorated within days; labs show **low phosphate, potassium and magnesium**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Insulin surge driving electrolytes into cells: **refeeding syndrome**.

elim: Glucose is 7.2; no ketoacidosis.
Glucose is normal.
No serotonergic drug, clonus or hyperthermia.
SIADH causes low sodium, not low phosphate, K and Mg.

steps.x: **C. Refeeding syndrome.** Starved + fed fast + low phosphate = refeeding.

technique.stem: A 79 year old man is admitted with pneumonia. He lives alone and his son thinks he has lost weight over the last 3 months. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. The ward nurse wants to identify whether he is at risk of malnutrition.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial assessment of his nutritional risk?

steps.x: 'Initial assessment of nutritional risk' means a screening tool.

clues: lost weight over the last 3 months
identify whether he is at risk of malnutrition
steps.x: At-risk elderly man; he is septic, so his low albumin reflects **inflammation** (CRP 186).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MUST**: BMI, unplanned weight loss, acute disease effect.

elim: DEXA measures bone density.
Albumin falls in sepsis, inflammation and liver disease.
Prealbumin is also an acute-phase protein and not a screening tool.
Waterlow assesses pressure-sore risk.

steps.x: **B. MUST.** Screen with MUST; never trust albumin alone.

technique.stem: A 55 year old woman has had extensive small bowel resection for Crohn's disease, leaving short bowel syndrome with a high-output stoma. She cannot maintain her weight despite oral supplements, and nasojejunal feeding has failed with ongoing high stoma losses. Her BMI is 16.8 kg/m². Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate nutritional management?

steps.x: A feeding route question: climb the ladder only as far as needed.
Oral and enteral routes have failed because the gut cannot absorb enough.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The gut cannot be used: **parenteral nutrition**.

elim: Fortification is a first-line oral measure; she is far beyond this.
Enteral feeding has already failed.
She is already on supplements.
A PEG still relies on a functional gut.

steps.x: **D. Parenteral nutrition.** Oral, then enteral, then TPN if the gut cannot be used.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man who lives alone has eaten very little for 3 months. He has bilateral pitting oedema to the knees. He has no breathlessness, the jugular venous pressure is not raised and there is no ascites. Urinalysis shows no protein. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his oedema?

steps.x: A mechanism question: why is this malnourished man oedematous?

clues: jugular venous pressure is not raised
steps.x: No heart failure, no protein in the urine, no inflammation: the albumin is low because it is **not being made**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Protein-calorie deficiency reduces **hepatic albumin synthesis**, lowering oncotic pressure.

elim: JVP is normal; no heart failure.
CRP is normal; no inflammation.
Oedema is bilateral and there is no mass or surgery.
Urinalysis shows no protein, excluding nephrotic loss.

steps.x: **D. Reduced hepatic protein synthesis.** Severe protein deficiency gives hypoalbuminaemic oedema.

practice.stem: An 86 year old woman is seen at home by her GP. Her daughter says she has lost 8 kg over 5 months and has stopped cooking since her husband died. She has had two falls. She has temporal muscle wasting, thin hair and a sacral pressure sore. Her pulse rate is 62 bpm and BP 110/64 mmHg. Her BMI is 17.6 kg/m².
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Unintentional weight loss, low BMI, wasting, falls and a pressure sore in a bereaved older woman living alone is malnutrition. TSH and glucose are normal.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a frail older woman with weight loss.

clues: stopped cooking since her husband died
temporal muscle wasting, thin hair and a sacral pressure sore
steps.x: Classic at-risk person with poor intake; signs of wasting, hair thinning and a pressure sore.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Malnutrition** from poor oral intake.

elim: TSH is normal.
PMR gives shoulder and hip stiffness, not wasting and weight loss with poor intake.
Glucose is normal.
Vitamin D deficiency alone does not explain the weight loss and wasting.

steps.x: **B. Malnutrition.** Elderly + alone + weight loss + wasting = malnutrition.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man with alcohol dependence has had diarrhoea and increasing forgetfulness for 2 months. He has a red, scaly, hyperpigmented rash on the backs of his hands and a band of similar rash around his neck. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which vitamin deficiency is most likely?
practice.e: Diarrhoea, dermatitis on sun-exposed skin with Casal's necklace and dementia are the Ds of pellagra, niacin (B3) deficiency. Thiamine deficiency gives Wernicke's or beriberi, not dermatitis.

steps.x: Name the vitamin behind the pattern.

clues: band of similar rash around his neck
steps.x: Diarrhoea, dementia, dermatitis and **Casal's necklace**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pellagra: **niacin (B3)** deficiency.

elim: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke's or beriberi, not dermatitis.
B12 causes anaemia and neuropathy, not a photosensitive rash.
Scurvy gives bleeding gums and perifollicular haemorrhage.
Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and osteomalacia.

steps.x: **B. Niacin.** 4 Ds + neck necklace = pellagra.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 1 year history of bloating, abdominal cramps and pale, foul-smelling stools that are difficult to flush. She has lost 6 kg. She now struggles to see when driving at dusk. Her BMI is 18.2 kg/m². Anti-endomysial antibodies are positive.
practice.q: Which deficiency best explains her visual symptom?
practice.e: Malabsorption in coeliac disease reduces micelle uptake of fat-soluble vitamins; vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness. Vitamin E deficiency gives neuropathy and K deficiency gives bleeding.

steps.x: Link a symptom to one deficiency.

clues: struggles to see when driving at dusk
steps.x: Coeliac malabsorption with steatorrhoea and **night blindness**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fat-soluble **vitamin A** deficiency.

elim: B12 deficiency causes anaemia and neuropathy, not night blindness.
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.
Vitamin E deficiency causes ataxia and neuropathy.
Vitamin K deficiency causes bruising and bleeding.

steps.x: **A. Vitamin A.** Night blindness = vitamin A; think malabsorption of A, D, E, K.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man with oesophageal cancer has eaten almost nothing for 10 days. Nasogastric feeding was started yesterday. Today he is weak and has palpitations. His pulse rate is 112 bpm, irregularly irregular, and BP 108/68 mmHg.

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: New fast AF after feeding started.

practice.q: Which is the most likely additional biochemical finding?
practice.e: Refeeding after 10 days of near-zero intake causes an insulin surge driving phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells; low phosphate is the hallmark. Sodium is normal here.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question after feeding starts.
Cancer, starvation, then feeding, then an arrhythmia: **refeeding syndrome**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low phosphate** (with low K and Mg).

elim: Magnesium falls in refeeding.
Phosphate falls, not rises.
Potassium is driven into cells and falls.
Sodium is given as normal.

steps.x: **D. Low phosphate.** The hallmark of refeeding syndrome.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has lost 15% of his body weight over 6 months after a stroke left him needing help with meals. He has generalised wasting. He has no breathlessness, the JVP is not raised and there is no ascites. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Severe protein deficiency lowers albumin synthesis and oncotic pressure, causing bilateral peripheral oedema. Palmar erythema, gynaecomastia and splenomegaly point to liver disease, which he does not have.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question in severe malnutrition.
Severe protein-calorie deficiency with a very low albumin and no heart, liver or kidney cause.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Peripheral oedema** from hypoalbuminaemia.

elim: Clubbing suggests lung, heart or bowel disease, not malnutrition.
Gynaecomastia suggests liver disease or drugs.
Palmar erythema is a sign of chronic liver disease.
Splenomegaly suggests portal hypertension or haematological disease.

steps.x: **A. Bilateral pitting ankle oedema.** Severe protein deficiency causes oedema.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man with alcohol misuse is admitted having eaten little for 2 weeks. Intravenous dextrose and oral feeding are started, but no vitamins are prescribed. Two days later he is confused and unsteady, with nystagmus and bilateral lateral rectus weakness. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?
practice.e: Feeding carbohydrate without thiamine in a malnourished alcohol user used up his thiamine, precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia). Sodium and glucose are normal.

steps.x: Cause of new neurological signs after feeding starts.

clues: nystagmus and bilateral lateral rectus weakness
steps.x: Carbohydrate given without thiamine; confusion, ataxia and eye signs: **Wernicke's**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thiamine deficiency** precipitated by refeeding.

elim: Withdrawal gives tremor and agitation, not ophthalmoplegia.
Hepatic encephalopathy gives asterixis, not lateral rectus palsy.
Glucose is 6.4.
Sodium is normal and has not been corrected rapidly.

steps.x: **E. Thiamine deficiency.** Always give thiamine before feeding a high-risk patient.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman with anorexia nervosa is admitted with a BMI of 14.1 kg/m². Nasogastric feeding is started slowly with thiamine. Her pulse rate is 48 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most important blood test to monitor daily in the first days of feeding?
practice.e: Refeeding syndrome drives phosphate (with potassium and magnesium) into cells, so these must be monitored and replaced. Albumin does not reflect nutrition or refeeding risk.

steps.x: Which test catches the main danger of feeding her?
Very high refeeding risk; electrolytes are low-normal now but will fall.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Phosphate** (with K and Mg) daily.

elim: Albumin is unreliable and does not track refeeding.
Amylase is for pancreatitis.
Ferritin does not change day to day with feeding.
Thyroid tests are not used to monitor refeeding.

steps.x: **D. Serum phosphate.** Monitor and replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman has lost 7 kg over 8 months with bloating, abdominal cramps and loose, pale, foul-smelling stools. She has iron deficiency anaemia. She eats a normal mixed diet including bread and pasta. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation for the cause of her malnutrition?
practice.e: Steatorrhoea, bloating, weight loss and iron deficiency while eating gluten suggest coeliac malabsorption; serology (anti-endomysial or tTG antibodies) is the first test. Calprotectin suits suspected IBD.

steps.x: Find the cause of malnutrition from malabsorption.
Malabsorption with steatorrhoea, iron deficiency and ongoing gluten intake: **coeliac**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Coeliac antibody serology** while she is still eating gluten.

elim: Colonoscopy does not diagnose small bowel coeliac disease.
CT is not the first test for malabsorption.
Calprotectin is for inflammatory bowel disease.
Breath tests are for lactose intolerance or bacterial overgrowth.

steps.x: **A. Coeliac serology.** Fat-soluble deficiencies and steatorrhoea point to malabsorption.

practice.stem: An 80 year old man is seen in clinic. He has lost 4 kg over 4 months since his wife went into a care home and his appetite is poor. He can swallow normally. His BMI is 19.2 kg/m² and his MUST score is 2. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Food-first approach with oral nutritional supplements
practice.e: A MUST of 2 or more is high risk: start a food-first approach (fortified, high-calorie, high-protein diet) with oral nutritional supplements. He swallows normally, so tube feeding is not needed.

steps.x: First-line treatment for a high MUST score.
High risk, but oral intake is possible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Food-first plus oral nutritional supplements**.

elim: NG feeding is for when oral intake fails.
TPN is only when the gut cannot be used.
PEG is for long-term enteral needs.
A high score needs treatment now, not yearly review.

steps.x: **A. Food first with oral supplements.** Start at the bottom of the feeding ladder.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has finished chemoradiotherapy for laryngeal cancer. He has severe dysphagia and cannot meet his needs orally despite supplements. Speech and language therapy expect this to last many months. His gut is functioning normally. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate feeding route?
practice.e: Oral intake is inadequate, the gut works and the need is long term, so enteral feeding via PEG is best. NG suits short-term use; TPN is only if the gut cannot be used.

steps.x: Choose the feeding route on the ladder.

clues: cannot meet his needs orally despite supplements
steps.x: Oral fails, gut works, **long term**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Enteral, long term: **PEG**.

elim: He already fails on supplements.
NG is a short-term route.
TPN is for a gut that cannot be used.
Thickened fluids will not meet his needs.

steps.x: **D. PEG.** Oral, then enteral (NG short term, PEG long term), then parenteral.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with alcohol misuse has eaten almost nothing for 9 days. Her BMI is 16.9 kg/m². The team plan nasogastric feeding. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to starting her feed?
o: Full calorie target with daily weights
Parenteral nutrition instead of NG feeding
Start slowly with thiamine and electrolyte replacement
practice.e: Low BMI, days of minimal intake, alcohol misuse and low electrolytes make her high risk of refeeding syndrome: start slowly, give thiamine, and replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium.

steps.x: How to start feeding in a high refeeding-risk patient.
Several high-risk features, and the labs are already low.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Start slowly, thiamine, replace phosphate, K and Mg**.

elim: Delaying worsens starvation.
Full calories on day 1 triggers refeeding syndrome.
Her gut works; TPN does not remove refeeding risk.
Carbohydrate drives the insulin surge.

steps.x: **D. Start slowly with thiamine and electrolyte replacement.**

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman with anorexia nervosa had normal serum phosphate on admission. Two days after nasogastric feeding with a carbohydrate-rich feed was started, her phosphate is 0.35 mmol/L. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 96/62 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her fall in phosphate?
o: Insulin-driven shift of phosphate into cells
Phosphate binding by the enteral feed
practice.e: Carbohydrate triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into depleted cells, so serum levels fall even though they were normal before feeding.

steps.x: Mechanism of hypophosphataemia after feeding.
Normal before, low after carbohydrate: a **shift**, not a loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Insulin** drives phosphate into cells.

elim: PTH is not the driver here.
The fall is a shift into cells, not renal loss.
Feeds do not bind phosphate.
Vitamin D deficiency would not cause a fall over 2 days.

steps.x: **C. Insulin-driven intracellular shift.** Starved cells soak up phosphate when fed.
